newsitem.title: MEXICO: New Mexican rebel group may disperse - radio.
newsitem.headline: New Mexican rebel group may disperse - radio.

text.p: A recently emerged Mexican guerrilla group, the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), may be forced to scatter its forces if government troops continue their crackdown in the south, Radio Red reported on Saturday.

It quoted an EPR commander with the nom de guerre Francisco as saying the rebels were not going to attack the army. He reportedly said that with the huge build up of troops in the area confrontation would be "social suicide."

The radio said Francisco's comments were made at a clandestine meeting with reporters in Oaxaca state, one of the home bases of the rebels who made their first appearance in the neighbouring state of Guerrero in June.
His comments come amid fears that the EPR, who carried out a series of bloody strikes against police and military posts in August, would disrupt Independence Day celebrations on Sunday and Monday.

Those fears were stoked by the discovery of a small bomb in Mexico's Monument to the Revolution on Friday. It was not clear who planted it. The EPR has denied planning attacks on civilians during the celebrations.

According to Radio Red, Francisco said the rebels killed 41 officials and wounded 48 during their Aug. 28 assault in several southern states. The government said 15 died and 22 were wounded in the fighting, including three rebels.

In a separate report, Radio Red said EPR gunmen appeared for the first time in San Luis Potosi, capital of the state of the same name in eastern Mexico, on Sunday. They left leaflets in a shoe box and hung up an EPR banner that remained for three hours before police tore it down.
The leaflets described the EPR as a "self-defence force" responding to state repression. The government says it is a terrorist organisation with little social support.

In the capital, Mayor Oscar Espinosa told reporters security had been stepped up following the discovery of the bomb ahead of Sunday's celebrations when tens of thousands are expected to gather in the main square to hear President Ernesto Zedillo give the traditional "Cry of Independence".
